speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I was moved to give the speech by having met many young people over the years, be it at my Meet-the-People Sessions or during my constituency walkabouts, house visits and other events in the Serangoon ward of Aljunied GRC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Current students, teachers as well as the alumni have also reached out to my volunteer team and I to share their ideas and suggestions which they often feel are not being reflected or heard at the decision-making level in IHLs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am proud of them for standing up and speaking up for the welfare and rights of their colleagues, their fellow students and juniors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this speech, Sir, I hope to share some thoughts and proposals that have been inspired by what they shared.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Which is why my speech will focus on IHL boards and management being more accountable, specifically to students and staff.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Against this, it could be urged that IHLs are not democracies any more than companies are.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why is there need for some degree of accountability and transparency about decision-making?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The reasons for why this is important may be self-evident to some, but I will spell those out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For one, IHL management, as with the management of any organisation may have blind spots to what students and staff need.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An example is how mental health challenges faced by students are very different from those staff faced and different too from those faced by older adults.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And unlike employees in a company, students cannot easily change courses or change IHLs, because doing so will have repercussions on their career progression.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must recognise that IHLs are not merely factories to churn out economically useful graduates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The part of their lives that students spend at IHLs is often among the most memorable, precious informative of their lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These experiences can help ground students and enable them to contribute to their communities in multiple ways later on in life, not all of which can easily be captured in dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ensuring that the environment in the IHLs is conducive to these journeys, in character formation, is vital to help ensure that those who pass through their portals become self-aware, self-actualised and socially engaged citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, being accountable means students and staff have greater ownership over their institution and have a better student experience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In economic terms, this could mean strong alumni engagement which may translate into better fundraising capacity downstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To cite one example of a concrete benefit, a good environment in a strong culture of accountability could also translate into the IHLs being more attractive to students and faculty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other words, it could be part of that IHL's competitive advantage and collectively contribute to our national competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As all IHLs seek to go beyond rankings and this is a goal that the Minister for Education has said he seeks, they should also build a reputation for being great places for students and this includes being more open, responsive and consultative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And perhaps, most importantly, enhance the accountability culture at IHLs help set the tone for creating such a culture across society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not think these incidents I am going to talk about are necessarily representative of the institutions they took place in, and it is definitely not my wish to single out any particular IHL for criticism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But these incidents serve of to give us a sense of what students and staff in IHLs feel could be some of the areas where the accountability culture can be improved.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A day later, a statement was put out that more hall spaces were opened up – the space for students on a guaranteed two-year stay guideline as well as international students who were already staying on campus then.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Student discontent with infrastructure can be found elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, out of the 30 halal options at NTU, I understand that many are vending machines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are also only a limited number of canteens out of the many at the residential halls that have halal stalls.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A media outlet interviewed students who said that they had highlighted this issue to the administration for some time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Buses at NTU are perceived by some to arrive irregularly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, wait times range from five minutes to 30 minutes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is my understanding that the NTU Students Union has highlighted bus-related issues to the administration in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another example which speaks of the staff experience during the pandemic, NTU initially made the decision to not allow students and faculty members stuck overseas due to border closures to attend lessons online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Students were asked to miss the semester and faculty members were asked to take no-pay leave should they be unable to make it back to Singapore physically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This affected students' learning, the teaching of faculty members, as many staff members have to cover for those absent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: NUS experienced similar issues of a perceived lack of accountability and transparency with the merger of Yale-NUS College (YNC) and the University Scholars Programme (USP).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The timeline for the implementation was short, with the announcement made in August last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is feedback from some students and staff that there was no transparency in the end game for the merger of YNC and USP at NUS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The decision-making process was seen by many as opaque and with limitations in the autonomy for working group student representatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some staff had similar feedback, lamenting that they were given little opportunity to participate in the process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, the then-President of Yale-NUS College commented that the decision was only shared with the governing board in advance of the announcement for information.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, some feel that the reason why infrastructural issues are sometimes not fully addressed is because there is no incentive to improve it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Students are not going to leave in the short run and will be forced to put up with this if they want to finish their education and receive their degrees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second broad issue is the perception of top-down decision-making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many students and faculty perceive insufficient transparency, consultation and co-creation in decision-making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, IHL governing boards often have absolute discretion over student union regulations and all decisions made by the IHL.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many students believe that the unions have little ability to seek structural or policy changes, and decisions are often made without consultation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was shown clearly in the case of the merger of YNC and USP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And when consultations are held, these are often non-binding, with the consequent decision-making being somewhat opaque.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The same transparency deficit may apply to disciplinary action, say, for sexual offences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The case of Miss Monica Baey is instructive and well known.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The reasons and the process behind why NUS meted out that punishment were not made wholly transparent to Miss Baey in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another individual university student has very recently gone public about a case where she was the victim of a sexual offence and she has publicly suggested reforms such as, for example, the university providing reasons for the disciplinary action taken and to offer the right of appeal to the victim.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The dismissal of Dr Jeremy Fernando of NUS' Tembusu College has also been seen in some quarters as not having been handled well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One last insight that comes through when reviewing this feedback and all these incidents is the perception that academics are insufficiently represented on boards of trustees, boards of directors or councils.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The view here is that the weightage of trustees who come from the education sphere can be increased vis-à-vis that of business leaders and civil servants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, the more well-informed views about educational quality, the faculty experience and student life quality could be brought to bear on deliberations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I reviewed the lists of the boards of Singapore IHLs and in most cases, I confess that I have some sympathy with this view.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think the weightage of educators and non-educators on these boards is an issue that deserves more study and thought on the part of MOE, perhaps drawing on international reference points.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope MOE can review these suggestions and work with our IHLs to encourage them to adopt policies along these lines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Doing so would be in the interest of the IHLs themselves, as it would enable them to enhance their competitiveness and attractiveness to students and faculty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my first proposal, I would like to talk about empowering rank-and-file faculty in university senates or oversight bodies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Typically, senates or president councils have strong representation from senior university administrators and less representation from the faculty rank-and-file.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could be seen as there being little separation between the president or provost and faculty members who can provide oversight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate this point with a question, do we know how many times other senate members succeeded in making the president or provost reconsider certain decisions in the various incidents I referred to earlier?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What roles did university senates play and what roles were they able to play?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In many universities across the world, it is not always or perhaps often that university administrators lead senates which are supposed to provide oversight over executive decisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Restructuring and opening up senates to more rank-and-file faculty could improve oversight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One area where this may be helpful is on the issue of academic freedom.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I filed a Parliamentary Question on this earlier this year, referring to the results of a survey undertaken among academics, which suggested that there may be a significant proportion of academics in our IHLs who feel concerned about the state of academic freedom here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The survey which, by the way, should be looked into and where further research to validate it should be done in the best interests of cultivating a strong academia here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This ensures that the voices of students and staff can be directly represented in the decision-making process, which in turn promotes inclusive decision-making that actively considers the views of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Even if student and staff representatives on the board are not given veto power, such a move creates greater transparency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The practice of granting student unions and staff a seat on the governing board is not by any means novel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's IHLs can and should do this too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In some universities, the governing board is required to have student and faculty members who are elected to that role by their peers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I propose mandating IHLs to consider petitions above a set number of signatures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For the university population, it legitimises petitions as a tool for policy change by providing certainty that such petitions will, at the very least, be considered by decision-makers at IHLs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For the IHLs, it serves as a filter mechanism that prevents unnecessary consideration of frivolous petitions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a move should prevent a repeat of what happened to students representing Fossil Free Yale-NUS and Students Taking Action for NUS to Divest respectively.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This raises the question of what number of signatures is enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Creating a requirement for IHL management to address petitions with a sizeable number of signatures would strengthen accountability and transparency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One happy side effect of such a system is that it may also help students learn about how they can be active and involved citizens in a democracy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, I propose simplifying the process for setting up new student interest groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For many students, campus life is a defining feature of their time in university.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Interest groups are one of, if not, the biggest contributor to a vibrant campus life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When students' interests and passions are not served by existing interest groups, they should be empowered and facilitated in setting up their own.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could the registration windows be extended or made more frequent or perhaps could registrations be accepted on a rolling basis, as is from what I understand, currently the case with SMU, but not the case with some other IHLs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could IHLs also make available to students a model club constitution so to speak, to make setting up a new group easier?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, for my last proposal, I would like to say that we need to learn from not just mistakes or gaps but also places of strength.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, when SMU was founded just over two decades ago in 2000 and was facing the challenge of how it should brand itself and create a school culture, it took only three years before they set up Singapore's first formal peer helping programme in a university.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was at a time when mental health for youths was nowhere near receiving the public and institutional attention that it now receives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a good example of how IHLs can make positive change quickly and effectively by just listening to the voice of students.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To take another example, I believe in the wake of the spate of sexual offences and sexual misconduct incidents in some of the IHLs, some IHLs now have a more robust approach specific to sexual misconduct but some have proposed further reforms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, Sir, our IHLs are to some degree a microcosm of our society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The environment we create there will have ramifications for the character development of our students, which in turn will play a huge role in determining the course that our nation takes in the decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The proposals I have made to strengthen accountability and transparency at IHLs would also set a good example for the tone we want in our wider society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By giving them more scope to make a difference in the IHL through feedback and activities like creating petitions, we would be better equipping and encouraging our IHL students to become better citizens of Singapore in the years ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Leon Perera has said many things, many of which we can all agree.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would say that we would also take a very nuanced position on some of the points that he has made.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, Mr Leon Perera's speech can be summarised into one of accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I agree we should promote accountability and I will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But before I go into that, I was a bit intrigued by Mr Leon Perera's many examples and yet he prefaced all his comments, that what he highlighted may not be representative of our IHLs' state.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I was not very sure if Mr Leon Perera meant what he said, or he accepts that what he said is not representative of our IHLs, and that certainly our IHLs have room to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I will take it in the spirit that Mr Leon Perera is trying to help us improve our IHLs' administration and what he says is not representative of the state of our IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I, for one, would be the first to agree with Mr Leon Perera, that all our institutions, IHLs included, have room to improve and we will certainly take into account many of the comments that he said.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: My next point has to do with, and let me clear the deck first, on some of the statistics and survey that Mr Leon Perera cited on academic freedom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I believe my Second Minister Dr Maliki Osman, had previously replied to this in a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I would be one to say that I will take all surveys very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When surveys say that we have done well, I remind my people to never let this get to their head.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When surveys say that we have not done as well, we do not take it to heart personally, but we always remind ourselves that there is room to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I always remind myself and my team that we should look at all surveys holistically and understand the purpose behind each survey, the scope of the survey and what it really tells us and does not tell us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I would suggest that we take all these statistics and surveys very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the ranking of our IHLs: some of the rankings rank us very well, some of the rankings do not rank us so well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And the difference is because they all measure different things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For us, as a portfolio of institutions, we must have the responsibility and the confidence to know what we are looking for in our IHLs beyond a narrow set of metrics – be it publications in selected journals and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It must also encompass student development, faculty development, how they use their resources well and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, that is my point on cautioning us to be careful about using surveys that measure partial statistics to reflect a wider point.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I would like to come back to what Mr Leon Perera led off with, which is the issue of accountability and participation by faculty and students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The fact that some students or some groups of students at some point in time did not get what they want, does not equate to a failure in accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It may be a failure to share, as the Member has suggested, the considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But to suggest that just because some people did not get what they want or have their needs fulfilled is a failure of accountability – that, I think, would not be how you and I would characterise the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I want to come back to this concept: very importantly, participation and consultation must not just be with select stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In any large organisation, be it in the Government or even in your Town Council or in our Town Councils or in any institutions, we must consider the stakeholder needs of the entire stakeholder group that we are dealing with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Make a considered decision and take leadership, responsibility to explain those decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Leadership accountability is not about just making nice speeches to try to make some groups of people happy and finding out that either it is inconsistent across time or inconsistent across groups.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, for many of the points that Mr Leon Perera mentioned, I would agree that there is room for our IHLs to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I want to make a distinction – to not say that just because of these isolated incidents, which in his words may not be representative of our IHLs, that therefore, they have not been accountable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We thank Mr Leon Perera also for his various suggestions on how our IHLs can improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Empowering the rank-and-file – we agree on that and in fact, indeed, many of our IHLs have mechanisms to consult their rank-and-file and make them participate in various decision bodies and decision mechanisms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That does not mean that just because they are not on the board, therefore, there is no such mechanism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They do not sit on the board but they give their feedback and there are different channels of feedback for different issues, for different levels of accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One example, if we are setting school fees, the responsibility of the management and the leadership must not just be to a certain group of students but to the diverse stakeholders, including the people who fund them and also, across the different generations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are issues where we can have more student participation, but there will also be issues which I do not think will be appropriate for student participation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I think we can agree on that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I do not think setting a number is necessarily the correct thing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: An issue that has many people chiming in to say that that is a good thing, does not necessarily make it the most urgent issue.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the other hand, an issue with very few or much fewer people chiming in also does not mean that that is a not an important issue.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What we need to do is not to go on in a mechanistic way and say whether this is or is not an important issue.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, the new student interest groups – I think this is an easy one.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We try to help people set up new interest groups and I like this, because I want students to take on leadership responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having said that, when you set up a group, just like the debate prior to the Adjournment Motion, we must have some rules on what should be supported and what should not be supported.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But in general, we agree with the spirit that we should have more students taking leadership because this is how they grow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Chan, you have about two minutes more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And my final response is that on the spread of good practices, you can be assured that it goes from the board level, all the way down to every level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Leadership is not just about saying the nice things to people to make them happy, without telling them the consequences.
